analysis.one_liner: Removes the Clean Water Act exemption for stormwater runoff from oil, gas, and mining operations.
analysis.headline: The bill, with 89 Democratic cosponsors, died in a House subcommittee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have lifted a special exemption that oil and gas operations (and mining operations) got in a 2005 energy law, which lets rainwater running off their sites carry pollution into streams without a Clean Water Act permit. It would have required the EPA to be able to issue permits for that runoff, and directed the Interior Department to study how oil and gas site runoff contaminates groundwater and drinking-water aquifers. The bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near oil and gas drilling sites, fracking operations, and mines — especially those whose drinking water comes from groundwater or wells below or near those sites. Under the current exemption, rain that washes across these industrial sites can carry sediment, chemicals, and contaminants straight into streams without any discharge permit, and affected communities have limited legal recourse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near drilling, fracking, and mining sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the section of the Clean Water Act that exempts oil and gas operations from stormwater discharge permitting, restoring the EPA's ability to require permits for runoff from oil, gas, and mining sites [S2][S3].

It directs the Interior Department to study stormwater contamination from oil and gas operations — measuring actual contamination, assessing groundwater resources, and analyzing how susceptible drinking-water aquifers are to pollution from this runoff — and report to Congress within a year [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas operators and mining companies, which would face new permit requirements, monitoring, and pollution-control costs for site runoff. Those costs could partially be passed to consumers through slightly higher energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Permitting requirements add compliance costs for energy and mining companies; supporters of the 2005 exemption argued that sediment from these sites is not the type of chemical pollution the Clean Water Act permitting system was built for, and that states already regulate construction and site runoff.

The bill's most concrete near-term effect was a government study, not immediate cleanup or new rules; the permit authority it restores would only take effect through EPA rulemaking, which could take years and face legal challenges.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, documented gap: a 2005 law carved oil and gas construction runoff out of the Clean Water Act's permitting system, leaving downstream communities without the standard protections other industries operate under. The cost is modest permit compliance for energy and mining operators, and the downside for the public is limited. The bill was modest in scope, though — the study provision would have produced information rather than enforceable protections, and the rest depended on later EPA action.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on March 19, 2015, with 57 original cosponsors joining on introduction [S3].
It gathered 89 cosponsors in total, all Democrats [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on the day of introduction, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators and mining companies are better off: the 2005 exemption that spares their site runoff from Clean Water Act permitting remained in place, avoiding new permit and monitoring costs. Communities near drilling and mining sites gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators keeping the permitting exemption

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to close the Clean Water Act stormwater exemption for oil and gas operations.

for.name: 89 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including all members who joined at introduction.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in the Water Resources subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 89 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-majority committee never moved the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have ended their Clean Water Act exemption for stormwater runoff, subjecting site discharge to permitting like other industries. The exemption was preserved when the bill died.
The bill also removed the stormwater permit exemption for mining operations, adding permitting and pollution-control requirements.

industries.industry: Communities and water users near drilling and mining sites
industries.note: Residents whose streams and aquifers sit below oil, gas, and mining sites would have gained a permit-based tool to address contaminated runoff, plus a federal study of aquifer susceptibility.
